pages.title: Welcome
pages.summary: The front page: what the notebook asks, where to begin, and every page by topic.

pages.title: What this notebook is about
pages.summary: Living things have been inventing new kinds of things for about four billion years, and they have not stopped. No computer world has yet been shown to do the same. This notebook follows one computer world, Graph of Life.

pages.title: How this notebook is written
pages.summary: How a page is laid out, what every page promises its reader, the rules of the research, and how mistakes are corrected.

pages.title: The ideas this builds on
pages.summary: Graph of Life puts together ideas from several fields: artificial life, game theory, network science, population genetics and statistics. This page introduces each one far enough to read the rest of the notebook, and says where it shows up in this world.

pages.title: A screen of random worlds
pages.summary: Round 1 of fifty worlds with every setting drawn at random found no healthy world and one interesting one: mended worlds are whole but folded, and the worlds that stay spaces break or are poor.

pages.title: Which worlds are healthy? Three orders
pages.summary: Round 3's living worlds in three orders of health: every measure scored by the share of the worlds a world beats, the six criteria multiplied, added or the worst of them; few tokens culled is the sixth.

pages.title: How the drawn settings shape a world
pages.summary: Each drawn setting judged on its own by shuffling: a cap of two links kills, gifts keep worlds alive, mending the dead spares a world its culls, and most settings show no effect.

pages.title: Candidates for open-ended evolution
pages.summary: Round 3's worlds read for heredity, selection and change: 72 candidates, evolution fast but narrow, and a shortlist of 24 from health's three orders, played again in Experiment 43.

pages.title: Did evolution happen? Fourteen ways to find out
pages.summary: Round 3's worlds pass on what their agents do and keep changing it, but with about fourteen ancestors sharing the future, luck can look like selection. Fourteen tests in six questions tell the two apart; eleven need no new runs, and the era tournament comes first.

pages.title: Did the brains get better? Round 3's eras against each other
pages.summary: Experiment 44, ready to play: in each of the 21 worlds of round 3's shortlist, the brains of every era played against those of iterations 250, 1,500 and 3,000, in the world itself; 1,512 contests. The thesis: most worlds got better early and had stopped by the middle of their runs.

pages.title: A hundred thousand iterations
pages.summary: A plan not yet played. Written on 9 October 2026 for one world of B1 at 204,800 tokens left for 100,000 iterations, it is now proposed again on round 3's candidates: three shortlisted worlds played on from iteration 3,000 to 100,000, which needs nothing new built and takes about two and a half days.

pages.title: The world: tokens, agents and a network
pages.summary: A world is a network of nodes joined by connections, with one agent on every node. Every agent holds a whole number of tokens and a brain that takes all its decisions. Tokens move between agents but are never made or destroyed, so their total, T, never changes.

pages.title: One iteration, step by step
pages.summary: An iteration is one step of a world's time: first reproduction, then the game. In reproduction, agents give part of their tokens to children, who join their neighbourhood.

pages.title: The brain
pages.summary: An agent's brain is a small neural network that takes all its decisions. For each candidate, the agent itself and each neighbour, it reads 154 numbers and gives 45, which the rules turn into decisions.

pages.title: Questioning the mechanics
pages.summary: Much of what the first baseline, B1, does follows from a few of its rules, not from what its brains compute. This page takes those rules one at a time: what each does, whether that is what was meant, and what could replace it.

pages.title: Is a run reproducible?
pages.summary: Every comparison in this notebook assumes that a run is decided by its settings and its seed alone. Experiment 1 tested this on three seeds, each run four ways to iteration 30.

pages.title: Every setting
pages.summary: A run of Graph of Life is fixed by two things: its settings and its seed (Seeds and the random stream). A setting is one number or switch of a run's rules, fixed before the run starts.

pages.title: Glossary
pages.summary: Every term of the notebook, from A to Z: what it is in one line, and the page that explains it.

pages.title: The rules in detail
pages.summary: The rules of a world, one detail at a time: how the first network is built, where chance comes in, how a brain's numbers become shares and decisions, what agents tell each other, how a coalition takes a node, how a brain changes, and when a world ends..

pages.title: B1 and B2: the two baselines
pages.summary: The two sets of rules every experiment starts from: B1, the algorithm as a new run is offered it, and B2, built so that its network cannot break.

pages.title: Building B2: a world that cannot break
pages.summary: B2, the notebook's second baseline, was built in three steps, each tested by an experiment. First, brains that see broke their worlds: not in one great cut, but by a steady bleeding of cut-off agents that births did not always replace (Experiment 13).

pages.title: Measuring lives: births, deaths, ages and estates
pages.summary: How the notebook counts the lives of agents: who is born and how, the four ways to die, where the tokens of the dead go, how old agents grow, and what every reproduction phase records..

pages.title: What keeps wealth spread?
pages.summary: Coalitions do not keep wealth spread: B1 without them is more even, because it turns over ten times faster, and in B2 and round 3 they change nothing. Where the estates of the dead go sets how unequal a world is, and the more tokens pass from the dead to the living, the more even it is.

pages.title: Measuring tokens: inequality and flow
pages.summary: How the notebook measures who holds the tokens and where they go: the Gini coefficient and its companions, what the game does when a brain scores nothing, and the flow of tokens along the connections..

pages.title: Measuring a network: connections, hubs, distances and cuts
pages.summary: How the notebook measures the shape of a world's network: how many connections agents have and how they cluster, the hubs and stars, how far apart agents are, and where a network can be cut..

pages.title: Physical inspiration
pages.summary: The rules of Graph of Life were chosen with physics in mind: they conserve the tokens, are the same everywhere, and are almost all local.

pages.title: Is a world a space? Dimension, and what folds it
pages.summary: The notebook's second aim is a world that grows a space of its own, like a plane or a room, from simple local rules. The worlds of the first baseline, B1, are spaces: about three dimensions by the room they hold, and two by how a random walker spreads.

pages.title: Measuring space: dimension and the random twin
pages.summary: How the notebook reads a network as a space: three ways to measure its dimension, and the random twin, the same connections wired at random, that every reading is set against..

pages.title: Dimensions at scale
pages.summary: Within one B1 world the dimension does not change with the scale beyond what a finite body shows: about 3 by balls and 2 by walks, as far as the rulers reach. Larger worlds read more over their first few steps, not because of their edge but because their hubs grow, and by their width they read four to five dimensions.

pages.title: Which properties have no scale?
pages.summary: Measured at eight sizes and rescaled, most quantities of a B1 world keep a size of their own, and the small cuts of a game average out. But the branches behind bridges and the pieces a game cuts off follow P(s) ∝ s^−2 up to the size of the world, so a game cuts off a tenth of a world or more as often at 100,000 tokens as at 10,000.

pages.title: Local rules only
pages.summary: A plan: the cull, the share-out and the one random stream each made local, one at a time, on six of round 3's candidate worlds against their own runs. Round 3 already shows that mending a death cut the tokens a game culls from 11.4% to 3.5% but not the big breaks, and folded worlds, and that estates flowing to the nearest living pooled wealth (a median Gini of 0.53, the highest of six rules).

pages.title: How far does a difference travel?
pages.summary: A plan: twin worlds that differ by one token moved between neighbours, played side by side from kept states of three candidate worlds, to measure the light cone (at most four steps a phase under local rules, which only 4 of the 24 shortlisted worlds would keep) and whether a difference grows or dies away, with heat spreading on the same network as the control.

pages.title: A source and a sink
pages.summary: A plan: tokens enter at one node, which passes to a neighbour only when it dies, and every agent pays a token an iteration that leaves the world, so the inflow replaces the total tokens as a world's one number. Tried on three candidate worlds in the local world, it expects a gradient around the source and a world that holds together without any cull.

pages.title: Particles: patterns that outlast what carries them
pages.summary: Patterns that keep their identity while what carries them is replaced, looked for in twelve worlds with three detectors, each beside a null and tried on a pattern known to be there: no ring of tokens outlasts the next stretch of games, no agent keeps a rhythm beyond a random walk's, and the groups that outlast their members are the network's own regions, which stay where they began. Only a world that froze keeps its patterns, as a crystal in which nothing is replaced.

pages.title: What holds a world's size
pages.summary: Every agent of a B2 world dies at the age of 100, so a world keeps its size only if one agent in a hundred is born each iteration. How eagerly the agents breed decides how full the world gets; with its tokens fixed, a full world is a poor one.

pages.title: What the brains are like
pages.summary: Every agent decides with a brain of 15,795 numbers, and we tested the brains of thirty B1 worlds at the end of their runs. They are nearly blind: a change in what a brain sees reaches what it does about a thousand times smaller.

pages.title: Do the brains matter?
pages.summary: Experiment 7 took away the brains of the first baseline, B1, in two ways, for the same thirty seeds. Worlds whose every decision was drawn by chance all died within three iterations, while worlds of random, unselected brains live: the brains matter.

pages.title: Brains replaced by their average
pages.summary: A plan not yet played: six ways for agents to decide, from chance to the world as it is, each played on from iteration 1,500 of five of round 3's shortlisted worlds beside the world's own replays. Its draft thesis expects that a world needs the way its crowd of brains answers what each agent sees, not who answers: a brain drawn afresh from the world's own at every look makes it itself again.

pages.title: How big should a brain be?
pages.summary: Round 3's brains of three to five tanh layers all respond to what they see, nearly 400 times as strongly as B1's, and depth costs them little; evolution raised their gain about as far as mutation alone would. The shape made no difference we can tell from chance to whether a world lived, how healthy it grew or how it evolved, so the smallest brain, three layers of 16, is enough for the next rounds.

pages.title: Measuring evolution: genotypes, eras and the open-ended test
pages.summary: How the notebook follows evolution: genotypes, families and the common ancestor; eras of a world played against each other; and the test, written down before the long runs, of what would count as open-ended evolution..

pages.title: Does evolution keep going?
pages.summary: Evolution keeps going if a world's brains keep beating their own past. So the notebook plays the brains of two moments of one world against each other, and holds the world's network to a health bar.

pages.title: How fast should brains change?
pages.summary: When a brain is copied, the copy is changed with a set chance, the mutation rate; in B2 it is one copy in five. Experiment 9 played fifty B2 worlds at five rates, from one copy in twenty to four in five.

pages.title: Every era against three
pages.summary: The notebook's two longest worlds are Experiment 18's, whose brains are mixed at birth, played to 50,000 iterations. Experiment 28 played the brains of every 2,500th iteration of each against the brains of three fixed moments: 2,500, 10,000 and 25,000.

pages.title: Assembly theory: how many steps to make a thing, and how many copies
pages.summary: Assembly theory counts the fewest joins that build a thing from parts and how many copies of it exist. Tried on the agents' neighbourhoods, its index turns out to be set by how many links a neighbourhood has, and the worlds hold about as much assembly as random networks with the same degrees. Over every world of round 3, a world's assembly follows a cap on links, not its health.

pages.title: Can a strategy written by hand beat evolution?
pages.summary: Evolution in B2's worlds slows down as they age: is the play it has found the best there is? To find out, we planted rules written by hand as a patch in evolved B2 worlds.

pages.title: What a brain can compute
pages.summary: A raider written in Python took 40% and 62% of two evolved B2 worlds, with play that evolution had never found. Yet 12 units of a B2 brain, with weights set by hand, decide as the rule does in all but eight of 62,114 situations.

pages.title: Why the raiders stopped winning
pages.summary: A raider written by hand took hold in young B2 worlds, but not in the same worlds grown older (Experiment 30). The worlds had not learned to defend themselves: their patches grew too poor, and a raider needs three tokens to take a neighbour of one.

pages.title: One agent in a sea of average agents
pages.summary: A plan not yet played: in a sea of agents that answer every look with a brain drawn afresh from the world's own, one agent planted as a leaf with a brain of its own, fixed and inherited (a brain of the sea, the world's main line's, or its future's), beside a marked agent of the sea in the same place. Its draft thesis expects that no brain gains by being an individual, and that none takes hold in more than one planting in ten.

pages.title: Who helps whom
pages.summary: Cooperation means paying a cost so that someone else gains, and in Graph of Life the only act is a stake. A stake helps a neighbour if, without it, the neighbour would have been more likely to lose its node.

pages.title: Do agents cooperate? Help, kin and partners
pages.summary: Cooperation means paying a cost so that someone else gains. In Graph of Life the only act is a stake. A stake on a neighbour's node helps if, without it, the neighbour would have been more likely to lose that node.

pages.title: Other contests: a lottery, and alliances
pages.summary: In the game of Graph of Life, a node goes to whoever stakes most on it. This page changes that contest in pilot worlds, two seeds each, and asks whether evolution then goes on.

pages.title: Gliders, and who helps whom
pages.summary: When an agent takes a neighbour's node with at least half of its tokens, its wealth and a copy of its brain move there together.

pages.title: Rules without numbers
pages.summary: B2, the world that cannot break, has seven numbers in its rules that were chosen by hand, and the notebook asks for rules without them. Taken away all at once, the numbers show what each was for: without alliances the worlds died out.

pages.title: Healthy and rich
pages.summary: The author's picture of a world that might keep evolving has two halves: a decentralised, resilient, almost three-dimensional network, and agents that differ in almost everything.

pages.title: Measuring health: criteria, the health bar and diversity
pages.summary: How the notebook judges whether a world is healthy and interesting: the author's criteria, the seven marks of the health bar that B2's worlds were held to, and the diversity score..

pages.title: Brains mixed at birth, in long worlds
pages.summary: Mixing a newborn's brain from its parent's and a neighbour's makes a B2 world smaller, so each of its agents holds more tokens.

pages.title: Who may be a mate
pages.summary: When brains are mixed at birth, a child's brain is half its parent's and half a mate's, but only the parent pays for the child.

pages.title: The candidates, played on and played again
pages.summary: A candidate world meets every mark of the health bar at iteration 1,000, and its agents are more diverse than B2's. Played on to 10,000 iterations, most did not stay there: of nineteen, five held, eleven fell back and three died out.

pages.title: Room and riches for the steadiest world
pages.summary: The steadiest world the notebook has, Experiment 19's, lives long and its agents differ, but it is folded: a small world, not a space. Experiment 31 gave it, one at a time, four rules that keep a world's room; each gave room and took something else.

pages.title: Every world side by side
pages.summary: Each page measures the worlds of one experiment or a few. This page puts every world in one table, measured the same way over the same stretches of iterations, and looks at them together.

pages.title: How runs are made, recorded and costed
pages.summary: How every simulation of the notebook is made and kept, so that it can be made again: the lab and the engine, what a run records, and what a simulation costs..

pages.title: How worlds are measured
pages.summary: A world of 10,000 tokens holds about 1,300 agents and lives 3,000 iterations: some four million agent-moments, recorded twice per iteration. The baseline worlds of 100,000 tokens hold about 14,000 agents for 1,500 iterations: some twenty million.

pages.title: One world, many colours: what the viewer can colour by
pages.summary: Statistics average; a picture shows where things are. The viewer draws a world as dots and lines, and colours them by any quantity it measures. Each value is placed on a colour map, within the range of the frame on screen.

pages.title: What goes with what
pages.summary: This page is an atlas rather than an experiment. It sets every quantity measured for an agent against every other, in twenty worlds. And it sets every statistic of a whole world against every other.

pages.title: Every simulation: what was run, and what was measured
pages.summary: This page lists every world the notebook has made. The lab's experiments were planned before they ran, and are judged against a thesis. The pilot batches are smaller sets of worlds that try an idea quickly.

pages.title: Statistics: the tools of the notebook
pages.summary: The statistics the notebook measures with, each explained from the start: medians and bands over many worlds, correlation and fitted lines, how long a world remembers, how sure a number is, how a spread splits into parts, and how many kinds a world really holds..

pages.title: What B1 is, and what stood in its way
pages.summary: The first baseline, B1, has been measured from every side, in thirty worlds of 100,000 tokens. All six theses written before its runs failed, and each failure taught something new about the world.

pages.title: B1: lives and wealth
pages.summary: The first baseline, B1, as measured in October 2026: a world's life, births, deaths and ages, how births build the network, inequality, gains and losses, and the richest and best-connected agents.

pages.title: B1: the game and its flows
pages.summary: B1's game and its tokens, as measured in October 2026: what agents stake and who wins the nodes, where tokens flow, and the groups they stay in.

pages.title: B1: the network, size and scaling
pages.summary: B1's network as measured in October 2026: its shape and core, how it breaks, power laws, how properties scale together, likeness at a distance, worlds of many sizes, and how much the seed decides.

pages.title: B1: brains, lineages and messages
pages.summary: Brains in B1, as measured in October 2026, and how alike the agents of B1, B2 and the pilots are: genotypes and lineages, the messages, and how differently agents play.

pages.title: What the switches did in pilots (indicative)
pages.summary: The engine's switches tried in pilot worlds in October 2026, alone and in company: indicative only, from two seeds a condition, mostly 1,000 iterations, on B2.
